props.title: Greed
props.initialSlug: Tale of friendship destroyed by lottery win

sections.content: Greed stands as Erich von Stroheim's masterpiece of psychological realism, originally running nearly 8 hours before MGM brutally cut it to under 2.5 hours. Based on Frank Norris's novel "McTeague," it follows a dentist's descent into murderous obsession after his wife wins the lottery. The film revolutionized cinema with its unflinching naturalism, shooting on location in San Francisco and Death Valley - unprecedented for its time. Von Stroheim's insistence on filming in actual locations, including the sweltering desert finale, set new standards for cinematic authenticity that influenced Italian Neorealism and later movements.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through decades of cinema examining wealth's corrupting power. There Will Be Blood (2007) echoes its study of greed-driven madness, while The Treasure of the Sierra Madre (1948) directly references Greed's desert finale. Von Stroheim's unflinching approach to human degradation laid groundwork for later directors like Sam Peckinpah and Martin Scorsese, who similarly refused to look away from humanity's darker impulses.

The legendary lost footage of Greed represents cinema's most famous case of studio interference. The original 42-reel cut reportedly contained intricate character development and subplots that made the tragic ending even more devastating. Modern reconstructions using still photographs hint at von Stroheim's complete vision, while films like The Magnificent Ambersons (1942) and Once Upon a Time in America (1984) suffered similar studio-mandated cuts. sections.content: Von Stroheim's brutal critique of American materialism influenced generations of filmmakers tackling similar themes. Wall Street (1987) updates Greed's messaging for the 1980s, while Blue Jasmine (2013) examines wealth's psychological toll through a modern lens. The film's technical innovations - including pioneering use of deep focus photography and location shooting - helped establish realism as a powerful tool for social criticism.
